author: Alex Kong
quote:
hey guys, I made a breakthrough on my trading and I wanted to share it.
You know how a lot of trading teachers say that most people just focus on what they can win but not on what they can loose?
Well, I finally figured out a simple way to manage my risk effectively.

For me, since I am starting, I have 3 simple criteria.
For A+ trades I risk $100, for regular trades $66 and for an entry position I risk $33
So, when I see something setting up, I determine the level of trade, then based on that I pick the strike price either the one ITM or one OTM, and if the cons are too expensive I go to the one above .35 delta.
Then once I have the con selected, I put my TP/SL chart, and I check the % of loss I would take. Then I input those numbers on this simple table
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1wN5CxVPSPw3opje_b1s5s-cEgqBwsER8bAlMU3awuMY/edit?usp=sharing
And that way I find out how many cons I can buy.

For example today I entered AMZN, the Contract was 2.20 with a max loss of 13.15%, which meant I could buy 3 cons for a max loss of $86.79 dlls, respecting my max loss.
And also putting in the Take profit % I can also know the profit potential of the trade before hand.
And that's it, you are free to make a copy of the spreadsheet, I hope it's useful for you, I believe this will be crucial for me moving forward.

Cheers everyone!

quote: I’m on TOS , can you please explain how to calculate premium so we can put the right stop loss?

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
quote:
Explaining Premiums and Setting Stop Losses:
Understanding Premiums
The premium is the price paid for an option, made up of:
Intrinsic Value: The difference between the stock price and the strike price (only applies to in-the-money options).
Extrinsic Value: The rest of the premium, including time value, volatility, etc.
Example:

If a call option has a $100 strike price and the stock is trading at $105, the premium is $7.
Intrinsic Value: $105 - $100 = $5
Extrinsic Value: $7 - $5 = $2
Calculating Stop Loss on TOS
Step 1: Decide Risk Tolerance
Determine the percentage of the premium you are willing to lose (e.g., 20-30%).
Example: For a $7 premium and a 30% risk tolerance:
Loss Amount = $7 × 0.30 = $2.10
Stop-Loss Price = $7 - $2.10 = $4.90
Step 2: Set the Stop-Loss in TOS

In ThinkorSwim (TOS), find the option trade and right-click on it.
Select Create Closing Order > Stop-Loss Order.
Enter the stop-loss price (e.g., $4.90) to manage risk.
This approach ensures your losses are controlled and aligns with your risk management plan

Here are 10 confluences for setting stop-losses effectively

Support/Resistance – Place stops just beyond key levels.
Swing Highs/Lows – Use recent pivots as stop points.
Order Blocks – Set stops past institutional zones.
Moving Averages – Use 50/200 EMA as dynamic support/resistance.
ATR Multiplier – 1.5x or 2x ATR to factor in volatility.
Fibonacci Levels – Stops beyond 61.8% or 78.6% retracement.
Volume Profile – Avoid high-volume areas where price sticks.
Trendline Breaks – Exit when trend structure is invalid.
Whole Numbers – Stops beyond psychological price levels.
Liquidity Zones – Avoid stop hunts, place stops outside wicks.

👉 Tip: Use 3+ confluences for stronger stops!

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
quote:
How to Set Up Key Levels & Support/Resistance Using Confluences

1️⃣ Identify Psychological Levels (Round Numbers)

Mark round numbers like $100, $250, $500, $1000, as these act as natural support/resistance where price frequently reacts.
Stops: Place stops beyond these levels to avoid getting wicked out.

2️⃣ Use Previous Day’s High, Low, and Close

Yesterday’s high/low often acts as strong support or resistance.
The previous day’s close can serve as an equilibrium level for continuation or reversal.

3️⃣ Mark Swing Highs & Lows

Identify recent higher highs (HH) and lower lows (LL) as key zones where price may reverse.
Stops: Use swing points as reference, placing stops just beyond these levels.

4️⃣ Look for Order Blocks & Institutional Zones

Order blocks (areas of accumulation before strong moves) act as key support/resistance.
Mark these zones where institutions likely placed large orders.
Stops: Place stops past the order block to avoid getting wicked out.

5️⃣ Use Moving Averages for Dynamic Support/Resistance

The 50 EMA and 200 EMA act as key trend indicators where price bounces.
If price is above the 50/200 EMA, they act as support; if below, they act as resistance.
Stops: Place stops beyond these moving averages for added protection.

6️⃣ Utilize ATR (Average True Range) for Volatility-Based Stops

Use 1.5x or 2x ATR to factor in market volatility and avoid tight stop-losses.

7️⃣ Apply Fibonacci Retracements for Key Reversal Levels

61.8% and 78.6% retracement levels often act as strong support/resistance.
Stops: Place stops beyond these levels to avoid premature exits.

8️⃣ Analyze Volume Profile to Identify Key Trading Areas

High-volume nodes = strong price attraction zones where price consolidates.
Low-volume nodes = price moves quickly through these areas.
Stops: Avoid placing stops in high-volume areas where price tends to stick.

9️⃣ Use Trendlines & Breakout Structures

Draw trendlines connecting swing highs/lows to find diagonal support/resistance.
Breaks of these trendlines confirm potential trend shifts.
Stops: Exit if the price invalidates the trendline structure.

🔟 Account for Liquidity Zones & Stop Hunts

Market makers hunt stops above previous highs/lows.
Stops: Place stops outside of liquidity zones to avoid getting stopped out before a reversal.

author: Lauren (lakatrades)
quote:
When traders talk about "1% per trade," they usually mean they risk 1% of their total trading account on a single trade. This is a common risk management strategy to prevent large drawdowns.

Breaking It Down:
Your account balance = $1,000
1% risk per trade = $10 risk per trade
Now, let's break this into options trading terms:

Step 1: Understanding the Contract Price
The contract price is $1.23, but in options, this represents $123 per contract because each contract controls 100 shares.

Step 2: How Many Contracts Can You Afford?
If you only want to risk $10 per trade, and the contract costs $123, you cannot buy a full contract without exceeding your risk.
Instead, you would need to adjust your stop loss to ensure your maximum loss per contract does not exceed $10.

Alternative Method: Position Sizing
Since one contract costs $123, it would represent 12.3% of your total account (which is much higher than 1% risk per trade).
If you strictly follow the 1% rule, you’d either need a larger account or trade cheaper contracts.

Solution: Adjust Your Strategy

If you still want to trade that contract:

Use a Stop Loss: Set a stop loss at a level where your maximum loss is $10.

Trade a Smaller Account Size: If possible, find contracts that are closer to $10-$50 to better align with the 1% risk rule.
Increase Account Balance: With $1,000, you may need to trade low-cost contracts.

author: Andreas Neuherz
quote:
hi all. I'm a junior in trading, though already a seasoned IT nerd. I had my challenges in sizing my trades, as though I had a certain amount of risk in mind, to be able to loose, though in reality, I always was looking on PnL and obviously, losing more than winning and getting caught, when picking the amount of contracts, who fit into my budget to spend, the risk size was never the percentage amount thought it should be or thought being defined. Like, willing to spend 1.000 USD and willing to loose 100 USD as values in my head, never fitted into the RR shown with the long or short tool on TV. After investigating a bit more and going through more of the lessons provided and rethinking all the influences of the process, kind of bulb showed up and my sizing approach was basically wrong. Why, well, if I take my 1.000 USD budget and buy 10 options, each at 1 U$, totalling to 10x100=1000, so far so good, though with the impact of delta and the potential risk defined,  gave definitely always a higher risk than my thought 100 US$ and gave me stress. Long story short, my conclusion was, too many contracts for the risk amount I defined for myself. So how to calculate the 100 US$ risk into the amount of options to buy? Well, nothing really special and maybe most of you already know, we usually take at the money or just out of the money contracts, they usually have a delta of around 0.5 which we need to multiply by the US$ move of the underlying into the stop loss direction and voila, this gives us the risk per contract and hence defines the amount of options I'm able to buy. Which means, in most cases, with my 1000 US$ budget, I won't need the complete budget for my risk I'm willing to spare! 
So to give me an easier way to show me the potential amount of contracts to buy, I modified an indicator I found on TV, the Position Tool and modified it, so it now provides me a table, how many contracts I caan afford to stay within my parameter. When I resize it on the chart, it automatically adjusts the table and of course, everybody can put in his default values. Unfortunately, I/you will need to put in your default values every time you put it on the chart, though you can reconfigure and resize anytime it's on the chart.
So in case, anyone wants to use it too, feel free: https://www.tradingview.com/script/v04WNCxq-OptionSizingTool/
